Working with World Ocean Atlas data

Source: vignettes/articles/working-with-woa.Rmd
working-with-woa.Rmd

The World Ocean Atlas (WOA 2023) from NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information gives long-term averages (climatologies) of ocean variables such as temperature, salinity and dissolved oxygen, on a global grid at standard depth levels. This article shows how to:

  • download a WOA file with woa_download();
  • find the variables and statistical fields in it;
  • read one field for a study area as a SpatVoxel, so that only that area is read from the file;
  • compare fields, read monthly climatologies and other variables, and measure a volume of water.
library(ocean3d)

Download a file

woa_download() downloads WOA 2023 files from NCEI and returns their paths. Files are kept in a cache (woa_cache_dir(), or output_dir), so a second call doesn’t download them again. The first time a file is written to the cache in an interactive session, you’re asked for permission.

f <- woa_download("temperature", period = "annual", resolution = "0.25")
basename(f)
#> [1] "woa23_decav_t00_04.nc"

You choose the file with three arguments:

  • variable: "temperature", "salinity", "dissolved_oxygen", "oxygen_saturation", "AOU", "nitrate", "phosphate", "silicate" or "density".
  • period: "annual" (the default), "monthly" (12 files), "seasonal" (4 files), or numbers: 0 for annual, 1 to 12 for the months, and 13 to 16 for the seasons January–March, April–June, July–September and October–December.
  • resolution: "0.25" (the default), "1" or "5" degrees. A 0.25° file is large (about 1 GB for salinity), so woa_download() reports each file’s size before downloading it.

Together, these make up the file name, woa23_{decade}_{code}{period}_{resolution}.nc: here decav (the average of all decades, the default for temperature), t (temperature), 00 (annual) and 04 (0.25°).

What a file holds

Each file holds one variable, such as temperature, as several statistical fields. Each field is a netCDF variable named {code}_{field}, such as t_an. Without var, as_proxy() lists them:

as_proxy(f)
#> Error:
#> ! Automatic variable detection requires exactly one data variable in each
#> netCDF file (coordinate and bounds variables are ignored).
#> File: woa23_decav_t00_04.nc
#> Data variables found: t_an, t_mn, t_dd, t_sd, t_se, t_oa, t_gp, t_sdo, t_sea.
#> Please specify `var` manually.

The variable codes are:

Variable Code Default decade
Temperature t decav
Salinity s decav
Dissolved oxygen o all
Oxygen saturation O all
Apparent oxygen utilization (AOU) A all
Nitrate n all
Phosphate p all
Silicate i all
Density I decav

The codes are case-sensitive: o and O, and i and I, are different variables. The fields are:

Field What it holds
an Objectively analyzed mean: the climatology, with gaps between observations filled by objective analysis
mn Statistical mean of the observations, only in grid squares with at least one
dd Number of observations in each grid square and depth
sd Standard deviation about the statistical mean
se Standard error of the statistical mean
oa Statistical mean minus the objectively analyzed mean
ma The period’s objectively analyzed mean minus the annual one (monthly and seasonal files only)
gp Number of grid squares with a statistical mean within the radius of influence
sdo Objectively analyzed standard deviation
sea Standard error of the objectively analyzed mean

For most analyses, an is the field to use, since it has a value in every ocean cell. dd, sd and se show how well a cell was sampled and how much the observations vary. The WOA 2023 Product Documentation describes each field.

Describe a field without reading it

as_proxy() describes one field without reading its values: the grid, the depth levels with their bounds, the time step and the coordinate reference system (CRS).

temp <- as_proxy(f, var = "t_an")
temp
#> class      : SpatProxy (experimental)
#> source     : woa23_decav_t00_04.nc
#> variable   : t_an (degrees_celsius), chunks 360 x 180 x 26 x 1
#> dimensions : 1440 x 720 x 102 x 1 (lon x lat x depth x time)
#> lon        : -179.875 to 179.875, 1440 cells, edges from bounds
#> lat        : -89.875 to 89.875, 720 cells, edges from bounds
#> depth      : 0 to 5500 m, 102 levels, shallow first, edges from bounds
#> time       : climatology, 1 step (months since 1955-01-01 00:00:00)
#> crs        : EPSG:4326

An annual file has 102 depth levels, down to 5500 m. Monthly and seasonal files have 57, down to 1500 m. A WOA file is a climatology for one period, so its single time step has no date.

Read a study area

A 0.25° field covers 1440 x 720 cells at each depth. Crop the proxy to your study area first, with terra::crop(): this still reads nothing, but it narrows what as_voxel() will read.

area <- terra::ext(-30, -10, 20, 40)
small <- terra::crop(temp, area)
small
#> class      : SpatProxy (experimental)
#> source     : woa23_decav_t00_04.nc
#> variable   : t_an (degrees_celsius), chunks 360 x 180 x 26 x 1
#> dimensions : 80 x 80 x 102 x 1 (lon x lat x depth x time)
#> lon        : -29.875 to -10.125, 80 cells, edges from bounds
#> lat        : 20.125 to 39.875, 80 cells, edges from bounds
#> depth      : 0 to 5500 m, 102 levels, shallow first, edges from bounds
#> time       : climatology, 1 step (months since 1955-01-01 00:00:00)
#> crs        : EPSG:4326

crop() takes an extent, a raster, a SpatVector or an sf object, such as a species range. It keeps the cells that overlap the area’s extent; to keep only the cells inside a polygon, mask the voxel with it after reading. An extent in the 0 to 360 longitude convention works on this -180 to 180 grid too.

as_voxel() then reads the cropped cells from the file as a SpatVoxel, one layer per depth:

v <- as_voxel(small)
dim(v)
#> [1]  80  80 102
head(depths(v))
#> [1]  0  5 10 15 20 25
head(depth_bounds(v), 4)
#>   depth lower upper
#> 1     0   0.0   2.5
#> 2     5   2.5   7.5
#> 3    10   7.5  12.5
#> 4    15  12.5  17.5

The voxel keeps WOA’s own depth bounds, the slab of water each level stands for, and its CRS (EPSG:4326). Because it has depth bounds, the bounds argument of volume(), mask() and the other 3D functions doesn’t apply to it. WOA’s bounds are halfway between its levels, which is what their default, bounds = "midpoint", gives anyway (see Depth levels and the slabs they stand for).

Compare statistical fields

Each field is read the same way. A short function reads one field of the same file for the same area:

read_field <- function(field) {
  as_voxel(terra::crop(as_proxy(f, var = paste0("t_", field)), area))
}
an <- read_field("an")
mn <- read_field("mn")
dd <- read_field("dd")
sd <- read_field("sd")

pick <- which(depths(an) %in% c(0, 100, 500, 1000, 1500))
area_mean <- function(x) {
  round(terra::global(x[[pick]], "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[, 1], 3)
}
data.frame(
  depth = depths(an)[pick],
  analyzed_mean = area_mean(an),
  statistical_mean = area_mean(mn),
  standard_deviation = area_mean(sd),
  cells_with_data = area_mean(dd > 0)
)
#>   depth analyzed_mean statistical_mean standard_deviation cells_with_data
#> 1     0        20.652           20.585              1.954           0.998
#> 2   100        17.807           17.840              0.732           1.000
#> 3   500        11.940           11.992              0.291           0.997
#> 4  1000         8.495            8.548              0.273           0.983
#> 5  1500         5.955            5.974              0.218           0.975

In this area almost every ocean cell has observations at these depths, so the analyzed and statistical means agree closely; in less sampled regions they can differ more. To keep only cells with observations, combine fields with terra, which keeps the voxel’s depths:

sampled <- terra::ifel(dd > 0, an, NA)
class(sampled)
#> [1] "SpatVoxel"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "ocean3d"

Monthly and seasonal climatologies

period = "monthly" downloads 12 files, one per month. Each is a climatology for its month without a date, so they can’t be joined into one series with as_proxy():

months <- woa_download("temperature", period = "monthly", resolution = "0.25")
as_proxy(months, var = "t_an")
#> Error:
#> ! woa23_decav_t01_04.nc has no dated time axis. Every file in a series
#> needs one, so its steps can be placed in time order.

Read each month on its own instead, here the mean surface temperature of the study area:

surface <- vapply(months, function(p) {
  m <- as_voxel(terra::crop(as_proxy(p, var = "t_an"), area))
  terra::global(m[[1]], "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[, 1]
}, numeric(1))
data.frame(month = month.abb, surface_mean = round(unname(surface), 2))
#>    month surface_mean
#> 1    Jan        18.94
#> 2    Feb        18.36
#> 3    Mar        18.21
#> 4    Apr        18.51
#> 5    May        19.40
#> 6    Jun        20.74
#> 7    Jul        22.08
#> 8    Aug        23.21
#> 9    Sep        23.60
#> 10   Oct        22.95
#> 11   Nov        21.60
#> 12   Dec        20.24

Monthly and seasonal files also have the ma field, the month’s analyzed mean minus the annual one. In August, the surface of this area is on average 2.55 °C warmer than its annual mean:

august <- as_voxel(terra::crop(as_proxy(months[8], var = "t_ma"), area))
terra::global(august[[1]], "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
#>                 mean
#> t_ma_depth=0 2.55339

Other variables

Every variable is read the same way; only the codes change. The code for dissolved oxygen is o, and its default decade is all:

o <- woa_download("dissolved_oxygen", period = "annual", resolution = "1")
basename(o)
#> [1] "woa23_all_o00_01.nc"
oxygen <- as_proxy(o, var = "o_an")
oxygen
#> class      : SpatProxy (experimental)
#> source     : woa23_all_o00_01.nc
#> variable   : o_an (micromoles_per_kilogram), chunks 180 x 90 x 51 x 1
#> dimensions : 360 x 180 x 102 x 1 (lon x lat x depth x time)
#> lon        : -179.5 to 179.5, 360 cells, edges from bounds
#> lat        : -89.5 to 89.5, 180 cells, edges from bounds
#> depth      : 0 to 5500 m, 102 levels, shallow first, edges from bounds
#> time       : climatology, 1 step (months since 1965-01-01 00:00:00)
#> crs        : EPSG:4326

Check each variable’s units on its proxy: dissolved oxygen here is in micromoles per kilogram.

Measure a volume of water

A voxel works with the rest of the package. For example, the volume of water between 10 and 15 °C in the study area, using WOA’s own depth bounds:

band <- occupied(an, fun = function(x) x >= 10 & x <= 15)
volume(band)
#> [1] 2004705

The volume is in km³. With the voxel’s own bounds, volume(band, bounds = "top") gives the same result.

Where next

  • woa_download() lists the variable and field codes, and as_proxy() and as_voxel() describe the proxy and how it is read.
  • woa_cache_dir() shows where the files are kept, and woa_cache_clear() removes them.
